title: Tako, the Octopus Who Played Piano, Retires After a Life of Music and Crabs
summary:
After months of viral fame, Tako the piano-playing octopus has officially retired. His owner, Swedish YouTuber Mattias Krantz, announced the news in March 2026, marking the end of an extraordinary experiment that captured millions of hearts.

The journey began with Krantz's longtime dream of teaching an animal to play piano. In March 2025, he visited a fish market and selected an octopus, naming him Takoyaki, or Tako for short. "I've always wanted to teach an animal piano," Krantz explained. "In theory, octopuses have incredible potential. They're as smart as a three-year-old, amazing problem-solvers, and each of their eight arms has its own mini brain. It's like having eight pianists in one body."

But the reality was far more complicated. Octopuses can't hear airborne sounds, so Krantz installed a vibrating speaker in the tank so Tako could feel the music. Since octopuses naturally pull objects rather than push, Krantz built a custom keyboard with pull-keys. To motivate Tako, he even rigged a "crab elevator" that lowered a live crab into the tank whenever Tako pulled the correct keys.

After six months of daily training, Tako learned to play note sequences. Krantz documented the process on his YouTube channel and released a documentary on November 5, 2025, showing Tako playing alongside Krantz's guitar. The video went viral, turning Tako into an internet sensation.

Unfortunately, octopuses have short lifespans, and Tako is now nearing the end of his. During this stage, octopuses naturally lose energy and sleep more. Rather than push for more content, Krantz turned off the cameras to let his friend enjoy retirement in his favorite tank cave. It's a bittersweet ending, but a fitting one for a creature who gave us a glimpse into the surprising intelligence of the deep.
why_it_matters: Tako's story illustrates the surprising intelligence of octopuses and raises ethical questions about using short-lived animals for entertainment, especially when human curiosity meets an animal's natural limits.

background_read: Octopuses are among the most intelligent invertebrates on Earth; they can solve puzzles, open containers, and navigate mazes, and researchers have observed distinct personalities and individual preferences in them.

Unlike humans, whose neurons are concentrated in the brain, octopuses have large numbers of neurons distributed through their eight arms, which helps explain Krantz's description of each arm as having its own mini brain.
Most octopus species have very short lives, often only one to two years, and near the end they enter a stage called senescence, when they naturally lose energy and sleep more.

Mattias Krantz (a Swedish YouTuber) had to adapt his teaching because octopuses cannot hear airborne sounds and naturally pull objects rather than push, so he built vibrating speakers, pull-key keyboards, and a crab-powered reward system.

The name Takoyaki comes from a Japanese street food made with octopus, which adds a playful layer to the name Tako and highlights how the project mixed science, creativity, and affection for a short-lived animal.

perspectives.description: Krantz achieved a long-held dream and shared a rare look at animal intelligence with millions of viewers. Tako's ability to learn note sequences inspired wonder about marine life and showed how patient, creative training can reveal hidden abilities.

Some may question whether keeping and training a short-lived octopus in a tank for online content is ethical, even with a gentle retirement. The viral fame may have created pressure that did not always center Tako's well-being first.

The experiment highlights how animal cognition is studied by adapting tools to an animal's biology, such as using vibrations and pull-keys. Tako's story is part of a broader pattern of internet-famous animals whose brief lives are shaped by human content demands.

Tako's retirement may encourage creators to treat animal stars more humanely and to share what happens when the cameras go off. It could also spark more public interest in cephalopod research and conservation, even as it raises questions about responsible animal content.
